walkthroughs.body_html:
Charge Q = I × t (amps × seconds). Moles of e- = Q / F.

Moles of metal = moles e- / n (charge on ion). Mass = mol × Mr.

Cathode: lower E° species reduced preferentially (e.g. H+ over Na+ in aqueous solution).

Anode: species more readily oxidised (lower E° for the half-reaction) discharged. Halides preferred over OH- if concentrated.

Anode: 2H2 -> 4H+ + 4e- (in acid) or 2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e- (in alkaline).

Cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. Overall: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Continuous source of fuel; only product is water.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
A positive E°cell means the reaction is exothermic in every case.
The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.

mcqs.q: If E°cell for a redox reaction is positive, what does that tell you?
options: The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — but it may still be very slow if kinetic barriers are high.
A positive E°cell guarantees the reaction will happen rapidly at room temperature.
A positive E°cell means the reaction is exothermic in every case.
Fuel cells burn fuel to generate heat which is then converted to electricity.

mcqs.q: How does a fuel cell differ from a conventional battery?
options: A fuel cell continuously consumes externally supplied fuel (e.g. hydrogen) and oxidant; a battery has a fixed amount of reactants that get used up.
Fuel cells and batteries are identical — both just store electrical energy.
Fuel cells burn fuel to generate heat which is then converted to electricity.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
